To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the economic value of probability forecasts is a function of the user's utility function and the probability of the event, (2) the economic value is a decreasing function of the probability of the forecasted event and (3) the economic value can be decomposed into a risk-neutral and risk-averse component.

the economic value of probability estimates depends on: the user's utility function; the probability of bankruptcy; the user's risk aversion; the user's prior beliefs; the probability of the event in question; the user's beliefs about the rival's probability; and the rival's beliefs about the user's probability.

(i) the economic value of a probability forecast is not simply a function of its misclassification rate; (ii) the economic value is not a function of the forecast's accuracy; (iii) the economic value depends on the utility function of the user, and the risk preferences of the user; and (iv) the economic value also depends on the utility functions of the other parties involved in the hypothetical bet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the economic value of probability forecasts, rather than the statistical properties of the forecasts themselves.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the economic probability score functions are a natural and intuitive way to assess the quality of probability forecasts.

the economic value of a probability forecast depends not only on the accuracy of the estimate, but also on the utility of the user, the risk aversion of the user, and the alternative forecast or betting price against which it is compared.

probability score functions are more than a technical device for summarizing the accuracy of a probability forecast: they are a way to evaluate the value of the probability forecast to the user of the forecast.
